setupSteps: Bar height: you should be able to start with straight arms, feet clear of the floor (knees bent) or just clear. A step up from a box is fine if the bars are high. No standard height was found.

Bar width: most guides suggest shoulder-width, or slightly wider (one guide says about 18-24 inches, 45-60 cm, vendor-level). Very wide grips force the shoulder into extreme rotation (elitefts). If the bars are adjustable, set them at shoulder-width plus a little, then change after one set if the shoulders feel pinched.
Bar check: grip the bars and push sideways; they should not wobble or twist. Report loose bolts to staff. Wipe chalk and sweat.
Clear space: nothing under or behind your legs; a mat or smooth floor to land on.
Stand between the bars, grip each bar with palms facing in (neutral grip), thumbs wrapped, wrists straight. On angled handles use the grip that keeps wrists straight.
Use a box or a small step to reach the top position rather than jumping up and swinging; sources allow a small jump, but a beginner should step up. Ask staff to stand nearby on the first visit.
Press up to straight arms, push the bars away and draw the shoulders down and back, chest up, so you hold the top ("support") position before any rep.
Legs: bend the knees and cross the ankles behind you (StrongLifts), or keep the legs straight if the bars are high.
Finish at the top with straight arms, find the box or floor with your feet, and lower your body weight onto them before letting go.
If you cannot finish a rep: do not drop into the bottom. Stop where you are, press up if you can, or lower slowly then step down; never let go mid-air.
Chest emphasis: lean the torso forward slightly, elbows slightly out (about 45 degrees to the body, RDL Fitness), hips behind.
Triceps emphasis: keep the body more upright, elbows close to the sides (ExRx assisted triceps dip page).
FitPlate start: a slight forward lean with elbows close, as one coaching source says this balances stress between the shoulder and elbow. Switch lean only when the form is clean.

steps.title: Step up and take the bars
steps.action: Stand between the bars on a box, grip with palms facing in, thumbs wrapped.
steps.visualCheck: Front: hands level and shoulder-width apart. Side: bars beside the ribs.

steps.title: Press up into the support hold (A)
steps.action: Straighten the elbows without locking them hard, push the bars away and draw the shoulders down and back.
steps.feel: Shoulders away from the ears; chest, triceps and front shoulder working.
steps.breathing: Breathe normally; never hold your breath.
steps.visualCheck: Side: arms straight, shoulders level with or above the hands, body still. Front: no hunched shoulders.

steps.title: Set the body
steps.action: Bend the knees, cross the ankles behind you, squeeze the glutes and lightly brace the stomach.
steps.visualCheck: Side: body in one steady line, no legs kicking out.

steps.title: Start the lowering by bending the elbows
steps.action: Bend the elbows slowly and let the body sink, shoulders staying down and back; keep elbows close (triceps) or slightly out with a slight lean (chest).
steps.feel: Triceps and chest lengthening under control.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbows go back, not flaring; chest does not collapse.

steps.title: Stop at about 90 degrees at the elbow (negative dip B and short-range reps)
steps.action: Lower until the upper arms are about parallel to the floor (elbow near 90 degrees) or as far as you can keep the shoulder blades tight, whichever comes first. Do not sink lower.
steps.feel: Stretch in the chest, no pinch at the front of the shoulder.
steps.breathing: Hold the breath for no more than a moment; keep air moving.
steps.visualCheck: Side: upper arm about level with the floor, shoulders not rolling forward past the hands.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Push the bars away and straighten the elbows, keeping shoulders down.
steps.feel: Triceps and chest drive; no shrugging.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbows straighten smoothly; hips and legs do not swing.

steps.title: Lock out and reset
steps.action: Reach straight arms and set the shoulders again before the next rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulders above the hands, neck long.

steps.title: Finish and step down
steps.action: At the last rep, rest at the top, find the box with your feet, then let go.
steps.visualCheck: Feet on the box or floor before the hands release.

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep. Why: the shoulder is pushed into end-range extension under load, which is thought to stress the front of the shoulder capsule and the chest tendon, especially when tired (review of the bar dip; evidence is mainly case reports). Fix: stop about 90 degrees at the elbow.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging into the ears
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging into the ears. Why: the neck and upper traps take over and the chest unloads. Fix: push the bars away and set the shoulders down at the start of every rep; if you cannot, go back to support holds.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging or kipping legs
commonMistakes.text: Swinging or kipping legs. Why: momentum hides weak strength and loads the shoulders and elbows in an uncontrolled way. Fix: cross ankles, squeeze glutes, brace the stomach.

commonMistakes.title: Grip too wide
commonMistakes.text: Grip too wide. Why: wide grips force extreme shoulder rotation (elitefts). Fix: shoulder-width bars or slightly wider.

commonMistakes.title: Elbows flaring or tucking hard
commonMistakes.text: Elbows flaring or tucking hard. Why: flared elbows add shoulder strain and tight tucking can overload the elbow. Fix: elbows near 45 degrees to the body.

commonMistakes.title: Rolling the shoulders forward at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Rolling the shoulders forward at the bottom. Why: the front of the shoulder takes the load. Fix: keep the chest up and shoulder blades tight; stop earlier.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure briefly. Fix: breathe out on the press.

commonMistakes.title: Jumping onto or off the bars
commonMistakes.text: Jumping onto or off the bars. Why: hard landing and loss of control. Fix: step up from a box, press up, step down onto the box.

commonMistakes.title: Switching to bench dips with hands far behind the body to "go easier."
commonMistakes.text: Switching to bench dips with hands far behind the body to "go easier." Why: the further behind the body the hands sit, the more the shoulder extends at the bottom; one source says the bar dip lets you change torso angle to keep the shoulder less extended. Fix: keep the back close to the bench and use the assisted machine or the support hold instead.

commonMistakes.title: Training dips every day or when the shoulder is sore
commonMistakes.text: Training dips every day or when the shoulder is sore. Why: recovery. Fix: 2-3 sessions per week with at least 48 hours between them (one coaching source).

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: dips load the shoulder into extension and rotation. Parallel dips are not advised for people with anterior shoulder instability, throwers or pre-existing elbow pain (elitefts); a review notes supporting evidence for injury is limited to case reports (including two chest-tendon rupture reports for the bar dip). Avoid with a tear, instability or impingement until a physiotherapist clears you.

Sternoclavicular (collarbone-to-breastbone) joint: no dip-specific source was found (Not found). General sources describe sternoclavicular injury as mostly from high-energy trauma, with spontaneous slipping possible in people with loose ligaments. Stop if you feel clicking, pain or a "slipping" feeling at the front of the chest.
Elbow tendon pain: pre-existing elbow pain is a listed reason to avoid parallel dips (elitefts); reduce range or use another push exercise.
Lower back pain: do not arch or swing; ask a professional.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table.
Spotter: not needed for the support hold. For negatives and assisted dips, have staff or a partner nearby the first time and a box under your feet.
Equipment check: shake the bars, check that the base is stable and not tipping, wipe chalk and sweat.
Gym etiquette: wipe the bars, do not hog the station between sets, do not film other members, ask staff before filming. A captain's chair on the same frame is covered in Gym 43.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); many are coaching blogs. The 160/90/60 degree elbow thresholds, torso-lean bands, 130 degree hip limit, 3 s minimum rep, support-hold and negative durations, and all sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: an ACE, Mayo Clinic or Harvard Health parallel-bar dip page; a professional-body prescription for support hold or negative duration; an authoritative dip-bar height or width standard; a peer-reviewed comparison of upright versus forward-lean dips (percentages quoted in blogs were not verified and not used); any dip-specific sternoclavicular injury source; the quoted Kibler et al. shoulder-capsule paper; condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, obesity, PCOS and shoulder problems.
